config.title: Missing Number

intro.title: Missing Number
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that finds the single missing number in a sequence of integers from 0 to n. You will learn the core concept of using arithmetic series to calculate the expected sum and compare it with the actual sum of the given array. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, arrays, and basic mathematical operations. This approach provides an efficient solution without needing nested loops, making it ideal for beginners to understand algorithm optimization.
intro.usecase: The Missing Number algorithm is essential in data validation and integrity checks across many applications. In inventory management systems, it helps identify skipped serial numbers in product batches or missing transaction IDs in financial records. Data analysts use this pattern to detect gaps in time-series datasets before visualization in dashboards. Form validation systems apply it to ensure sequential numbering in document tracking or order processing workflows. This algorithm provides the foundation for reliable data quality checks in enterprise software.

objectives: Implement a function that calculates the expected sum of a complete sequence of numbers.
Apply a loop to compute the actual sum of a given array of integers.
Construct a solution that returns the missing number by comparing expected and actual sums.
Manipulate array inputs to handle edge cases such as empty or single-element arrays.
Initialize and update variables to track sums during iteration.
Integrate the missing number function into a testable code structure.
Control the function's logic to correctly identify the missing integer in O(n) time.

content.body: Sometimes numbers go missing! In this lesson, you'll find the one number that's absent from a sequence. We'll learn a clever way to track what we've seen using a simple lookup structure.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply a hash map to remember which numbers we've encountered.
• Implement a single-pass solution to find the missing number.
• Explain why checking a lookup is faster than scanning the array repeatedly.
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: Look at this tiny array: [0, 1, 3]. Which number is missing from the sequence 0,1,2,3?

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: Now look at [3, 0, 1]. Which number is missing from 0,1,2,3?
content.successMessage: Correct! 2 is still missing, even though the numbers are jumbled.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: What about [9, 6, 4, 2, 3, 5, 7, 0, 1]? Which number is missing from 0 through 9?
content.successMessage: Great! You scanned and found that 8 is missing. You mentally checked off each number as you saw it.

content.body: You just did a mental scan: for each expected number, you looked through the array to see if it was there. That's like checking a list over and over—it works but gets slow for big arrays.
content.title: What you did

content.body: If the array has 10,000 numbers, scanning for each possible number becomes very inefficient. We need a way to remember what we've seen in one pass. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The core idea is to remember what we have already seen. Instead of rescanning, we can use a lookup structure (like an object or Map) to note each number we encounter. Then, we can check in one step whether a number exists.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it as a notebook where we write down each number we see. Later, we just flip through the notebook to see if a number is written, instead of searching the whole array again.

content.body: We'll walk through the array once, adding each number to our lookup. Then, we'll check which expected number is not in the lookup.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Create an empty object to act as our lookup (notebook).
2. Loop through each number in the array.
3. For each number, add it as a key in the lookup object.
4. Loop through all expected numbers (from 0 to array length).
5. For each expected number, check if it exists as a key in the lookup.
6. The first expected number not found is the missing one.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called missingNumber that takes an array nums as a parameter.
steps.hint: Start with the function keyword and a parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the function is named missingNumber and takes one parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a function named missingNumber that accepts an array.

steps.title: Create the lookup object
steps.instruction: Inside the function, create an empty object called seen to store numbers we encounter.
steps.expectedOutcome: An empty object declared inside the function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Now we have a place to remember seen numbers.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Declare a variable 'seen' and set it to an empty object.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember, we need an empty object to act as our lookup notebook.

steps.title: Fill the lookup
steps.instruction: Loop through the nums array and add each number as a key to the seen object.
steps.hint: Use a for...of loop and assign seen[num] = true.
steps.expectedOutcome: A loop that populates the seen object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your loop syntax and make sure you're adding each num to seen.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to iterate through nums and store each number in seen.

steps.title: Find the missing number
steps.instruction: After the loop, check each expected number from 0 to nums.length. Return the first one that's not in seen.
steps.hint: Use another loop and check if (!seen[i]) return i;
steps.expectedOutcome: A loop that returns the missing number.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Loop through expected numbers and return when one is missing from seen.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to check numbers 0 through nums.length and return the missing one.

content.body: Great work! You've implemented a hash map solution for the Missing Number lesson. Remember: the lookup object lets us remember what we've seen in one pass, avoiding repeated scans. This pattern—using a structure to track seen items—is powerful for many array lessons.
content.title: Done
